articles.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
articles.titleZh: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
articles.summary: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security

blocks.text: 21st October 2026 - Link Blog

Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security (via) If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process.
This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong:

On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...]
As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.
This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure:

August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.
August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.
August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.
September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.
October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.
October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.

articles.titleZh: Panache — RTS Belle Époque pour mobile
articles.summary: Panache — RTS Belle Époque pour mobile

blocks.text: 21st October 2026 - Link Blog

Panache — RTS Belle Époque pour mobile (via) Well this is delightful: I released Battle Drones yesterday under an Apache 2.0 License and there's already a French language fork which reskins the game to take place in steampunk 1900s France and adds an animated intro!

Panache est un jeu de stratégie en temps réel pour mobile et navigateur, dans la France de la Belle Époque (vers 1900) : dirigeables, Fardiers à vapeur, Creusot cuirassés, automates en képi, Gargantua la forteresse marchante — et beaucoup de panache.
You can play Panache here - it's worth clicking that link just to experience the new intro video.
So far it's mostly just aesthetic updates as opposed to gameplay changes. The music has had a French twist added to it as well.
The new steampunk models are so cool!
Here's a page with the original Battle Drones models and that same page with the new Panache alternatives.
This is a comparison of the original and the new design for the Goliath:
20th October 2026 - Link Blog
eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise. This is very, very bad news:

The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages.
In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists.

articles.title: Upgrade your PHP installs immediately to protect against php2shell
articles.titleZh: Upgrade your PHP installs immediately to protect against php2shell
articles.summary: Upgrade your PHP installs immediately to protect against php2shell

blocks.text: This morning, two critical PHP Security Advisories were published:
RCE via OOM corruption (9.2/10)
RCE via stale global state (9.2/10)

If you're running PHP for any service, you need to upgrade immediately to 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12. And if you use Remi's repos on RedHat-derivative Linux distros, you need to switch to official repos temporarily as Remi's on vacation and can't update his community repo. (Reminds me of xkcd 2347).

I'm glad I finished migrating this website from a PHP-based CMS to Hugo earlier this year—having a static website and a minimal commenting system saves on hosting costs and dramatically reduces attack surfaces. Especially in this era of AI tooling making exploit discovery easier.
Speaking of, Wiz.io released their report on the discovery of the exploits, which take advantage of OOM errors and PHP's fault handling code going back 20 years.

Within a few hours of people spreading the word about the bugs yesterday, some people were demonstrating exploits in the wild, leading to many sites switching off their public-facing services entirely, until they could upgrade.
Between this and the eMudhra certificate compromise, it's been a busy week in the infrastructure world...

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.titleZh: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.summary: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

blocks.text: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

blocks.text: For a software developer position, there isn't a trick to finding the best candidate. Your criteria do not determine how solid the candidates will be. Everyone is submitting 500 applications a month now, and those who automate the process submit thousands.

So how do you hire a great candidate? Pick a few from the lot, ask them if they can write a function, have them do a live FizzBuzz test, then ask them to deploy a service from localhost to an actual public server. That's it. Hire them after that.

As far as experience is concerned, they will learn on the job. If you think they don't know how to write tests or use a particular paradigm, they can ask ChatGPT and apply what it tells them a few times until they get familiar with it. People learn on the job. Nobody knows what the hell back pressure is until they encounter it in a particular service.
Everything else is really just random. We insist on things like culture, but we have no way of measuring it. It's all so arbitrary.

For example, early in my career I had an in-person interview where the head of HR brought me close to tears. She would make a joke, I would laugh, and while I was laughing she would stop and vigorously take notes. While she wrote, she would casually ask, "Why do you look so stressed out?" I nearly choked. I had just lost my father, and I had rescheduled the first interview so I could bury him.

The VP of engineering pulled a similar stunt on me. I did 6 interviews in 3 days, and they called me for a 7th. I lay on my bed, ready to give up. But I had a whole family to take care of and a giant shoe to fill, so I decided to do it. That same evening, I got an email saying the interview was cancelled; instead, they were ready to hire me. I didn't know whether I was supposed to be happy or mad.

It took 2 years on the job to figure out why they had done this to me. The person I was hired to replace had gone from a great employee to a complete psycho. Once, a teammate made the mistake of rejecting his PR. When he saw the rejection, he got up from his desk, climbed over the cubicles, and walked from desk to desk all the way to her cubicle. With his foot on her screen, he said, "What the fuck did you just do?"

So I learned that the culture and psychological test I was put through was meant to filter out this type of person. It could have been called a success, because I was well liked and never threatened anyone in my 4-year tenure at the company. However, that same test couldn't stop them from hiring two employees who ended up being convicted of murder. One of them had a well-televised trial and is currently serving life without parole.
So those culture interviews are only designed to please a manager somewhere. They have no documented effectiveness.
On Reddit's recruiting hell topic, you'll find mind-blowing stories of candidates being rejected for no good reason.
You might ask:
“What about experts? Surely the bar is higher than just writing a function, right?”

It's much easier to find an expert than people tend to admit. If you sort through your resume list right now and use only the criterion of 10-plus years in the field, you'll have your expert. Pick one, ask them to talk about their field of expertise, then hire them. If you're afraid they might not be the best candidate, I'm afraid to say that there is no way to determine that before they start working for you.
The problem is that companies want those experts at the price of an undergrad. Or they think they need to build the next Google when they run a small business with a manageable number of customers.
Hiring is only hard because we approach it like a dating app. We have unrealistic criteria for made-up scenarios. If they can write a function, you can hire them.

articles.title: Why didn’t we use Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown to clean up the unmarshalable delegate?
articles.titleZh: Why didn’t we use Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown to clean up the unmarshalable delegate?
articles.summary: Why didn’t we use Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown to clean up the unmarshalable delegate?

blocks.text: In my attempt to  create a fake agile wrapper that is technically agile but is not useful outside its home apartment,  Luca Bacci suggested, among other things, using the Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown function.
The Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown function is nice, but it doesn’t suit our needs.

One problem is that the object registered for apartment shutdown must be agile. (If you pass a non-agile object, the call fails.) That means that our wrapper must be agile. If we put the non-marshalable non-agile object inside our wrapper, we now have an agile object (the wrapper) that holds a non-agile object (the original object) as a member, which creates the risk that the wrapper will run down in the wrong apartment. The normal way of fixing that is to use Ro­Get­Agile­Reference to create an agile wrapper around the non-agile object, and store that agile wrapper in our container object.
This puts us back where we started: We are trying to implement that agile wrapper!

Even if we got past that problem, we have another problem: At apartment shutdown, COM calls the wrapper object’s UnInitialize method, and there’s a warning on the using the Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown function:
Warning: Don’t call the Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown function from the OnUninitialize callback.

But wait, what if the destructor of the object we are wrapping wants to call Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown? It might happen indirectly because it has its own reference to another object, that in turn tries to call Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown.

For example, it might hold another fake agile wrapper whose UnInitialize method has already been called! (We can work around that in our agile wrapper by nulling out the non-agile pointer so we don’t double-release, but maybe there’s some other object that uses Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown that is less resilient to this scenario.)

Another requirement of Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown is that it must be called from the same apartment that registered. This doesn’t quite put us back where we started, but it makes things more complicated because the whole point of the exercise is to find a way to release the object without having to try to switch to the apartment. I guess what we could do is use IContext­Callback to try to switch back to the apartment to release the original object and unregister the apartment shutdown callback. If the apartment switch fails, then we assume it’s because the apartment has already run down, so we assume that the IApartment­Shutdown::On­Uninitialize method was called, and it released the object for us. (Of course, that still creates the problem that we are cleaning up inside the On­Uninitialize callback, which meas that nobody else can unregister their apartment shutdown callback.)

The last note on this is that the implementation is written on the assumption that there are not a lot of apartment shutdown callbacks. Registration is O(1), but unregistration is O(n) because it does a linear search through all of the apartment’s registered shutdown callbacks to find the one being unregistered. By comparison, the Global Interface Table is designed on the assumption that it will have to manage a lot of objects, so it can look up its cookies in O(1) time. The proposed alternate design would register and unregister a lot of apartment shutdown callbacks, so it’s pushing the apartment shutdown callback list into a usage pattern it wasn’t optimized for.
Author

Raymond has been involved in the evolution of Windows for more than 30 years. In 2003, he began a Web site known as The Old New Thing which has grown in popularity far beyond his wildest imagination, a development which still gives him the heebie-jeebies. The Web site spawned a book, coincidentally also titled The Old New Thing (Addison Wesley 2007). He occasionally appears on the Windows Dev Docs Twitter account to tell stories which convey no useful information.

blocks.text: The NIST elliptic curves have been in the news twice lately. A few days ago Anthropic posted a paper on the NIST curve seeds that I wrote about here. Now the curves are in the news again, this time over broken certificates.

My post a few days ago was about the possibility that the NSA had added a backdoor to the NIST curves. Anthropic researchers showed that this wasn’t the case. The NSA had not been able to defend how the curve seeds were chosen because they forgot, but researchers from Anthropic were able to reverse engineer the source of the seeds.

So apparently the NIST curves do not have a backdoor, but as with all encryption, the Achilles heel is human error. eMudrha was using the NIST curve P-384  with extremely small keys: 4, 56, 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. To understand why this is a problem, I’ll briefly describe how elliptic curve cryptography works.
P-384 is an elliptic curve designed by NIST, with input from the NSA, for use in cryptography. The curve has on the order of 2384 points [1] because the base field is the integers mod

blocks.text: I was watching a video by John Higgins this morning about the poem in Ecclesiastes 3, one of the most famous passages in the Bible.

There is a time for everything,
and a season for every activity under the heavens:
a time to be born and a time to die,
a time to plant and a time to uproot,
a time to kill and a time to heal,
a time to tear down and a time to build,
a time to weep and a time to laugh,
a time to mourn and a time to dance,
a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them,
a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,
a time to search and a time to give up,
a time to keep and a time to throw away,
a time to tear and a time to mend,
a time to be silent and a time to speak,
a time to love and a time to hate,
a time for war and a time for peace.
The poem has a great deal of symmetry, from birth and death to war and peace. It has seven couplets, and the number seven in the Bible is symbolic of perfection.
There is a repeated pattern of groups of four words: a time for X, a time for Y. The rhythm reminds me of Beethoven’s fifth symphony, especially the third movement [1].
Higgins points out that there’s something odd in the middle couplet:

a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them,
a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,

It breaks the rhythm, at least in English translation, and presumably in the original language. The poem goes from intransitive adjectival infinitives —to plant, to uproot, etc.—to transitive—to gather stones. Also, the two parts of the couplet do not obviously fit together. There’s a similarity between birth and planting, between killing and tearing down, etc. But what’s the connection between casting stones and embracing?

Higgins explains that this deliberate symmetry breaking fits the theme of the Ecclesiastes as a whole. There is order to the world, and yet we don’t have it all figured out. Even when everything mostly makes sense, there’s something we don’t understand, like the middle couplet.

[1] This has been called the fate motif. There is an apocryphal story that Beethoven described it as such to his secretary and biographer Anton Schindler. Regardless of whether the story is true, the name stuck. Here’s the particular part I had in mind.

blocks.text: eMudhra generated eight of its intermediate CA certificates incorrectly, so their private keys can be recovered from the certificates themselves. Firefox (OneCRL and CRLite) and Chrome (CRLSets) blocked the intermediates on 17 October, Apple on the 19th, and Microsoft on the 20th through Windows’ automatic trust list updates. The disclosure page states that “many other clients do not consume revocation information and require software updates”, and its fix table lists the packages that carry their own copy of the roots:
certifi 2026.10.19 and pip 26.2.2
uv 0.13.4 and pixi 0.82.1
webpki-roots and webpki-root-certs 1.0.10, rustls-webpki 0.103.16, rustup 1.29.2
Composer’s ca-bundle, Elixir’s castore 1.0.22, Perl’s Mozilla::CA 20261020
the curl CA bundle, NSS 3.131.1, and a row of Linux distributions
the pip3 shipped with macOS, which uses “its own outdated copy of the roots”

Michał Górny, who maintains a large part of Gentoo’s Python packaging, traced where certifi alone ends up. Gentoo’s certifi is patched to use the system store, so system Python picks up the change when ca-certificates updates. Everywhere else needs its own update:
Each virtualenv and conda environment that installs certifi has its own copy.
pip vendors certifi, so every environment’s pip needs upgrading, using the old pip to fetch the new one.
Python vendors pip through ensurepip to bootstrap new environments, so anywhere ensurepip installs its bundled wheel you wait for a Python release, or upgrade pip after every python -m venv.
Lockfiles need certifi bumped, and dependency cooldowns need an exception for it, because a cooldown on a trust store delays the fix.
Rust tools like uv compile webpki-roots into the binary, so each one needs a rebuild and a release, and so does any container image that includes them.
Flatpak runtimes each carry their own ca-certificates, and some Flatpak apps carry another copy inside that.
Bundles in critical packages

To find the routes beyond the well-known ones, I pointed git-pkgs/certs at the 6,877 packages that ecosyste.ms marks as critical across PyPI, npm, crates.io, Go, Maven Central, Packagist, NuGet and RubyGems. It downloads each package archive, reads every file statically, and pulls out anything that parses as an X.509 certificate. 116 of those packages contained certificates, about 1.7%, mostly test fixtures and package-signing certs. 28 of them ship something that works as a CA bundle. A separate RubyGems sample added a 29th, honeybadger, from outside the critical list. The full results for all 29 give each package’s version and how it loads its bundle.

The real number may be higher, because the scanner reads PEM, DER, JKS and PKCS#12 and skips certificates compiled into native code, and 49 of the 50 platform-specific Python wheels in the sample contained compiled binaries outside those formats. Across the 29, the same cacert.pem sets the trusted roots for every TLS connection in some packages and is loaded only on request, or not at all, in others:
Excon, pip and redshift-connector load their bundle alongside the system roots. A root removed from the OS store stays trusted, because the bundle adds it back.

Stripe’s Ruby library and httpclient on MRI build their own OpenSSL::X509::Store from the bundle and hand it to the connection, so a ca-certificates update leaves them trusting the same roots as before.

Honeybadger, aws-sdk-v1, Guzzle 3, stripe-php and braintree_php point OpenSSL or curl at their own file by default, and a configured path overrides it. gRPC’s Ruby, PHP and Python packages register their bundled roots as the default.

botocore and the AWS CLI use their bundled file when certifi is absent. httplib2 uses its own after checking configured paths, and two of Google’s Java clients fall back to a bundled keystore when the Java installation store is missing. Whether a given deployment hits the fallback depends on what else is installed there.

aws-sdk-core uses system roots by default and switches to its bundle when you call Aws.use_bundled_cert!, and gocertifi, Composer’s ca-bundle and ioredis’s RedisCloud profile likewise take effect only when code selects them. nap uses its bundled file once the caller turns on certificate verification.

libv8 carries a bundle inside its vendored copy of depot_tools, and App Engine’s API stubs use theirs for the local development server. virtualenv’s embedded pip wheels each contain a certifi. These ship to every install and are separate from an application’s own HTTPS requests, except that virtualenv installs its wheels as the pip in each environment it creates.
Removed roots

Matching the certificate sets against historical Mozilla releases dates honeybadger’s bundle to 2011 and httpclient’s to 2014 or 2015. Both gems are maintained: httpclient 2.9.0 came out in February 2025 and honeybadger 6.9.3 in September 2026, and both releases still ship those bundles.

Algoliasearch, aws-sdk-v1 (last released in April 2017) and Guzzle 3 (whose repository is archived) still contain StartCom roots that Mozilla removed in Firefox 58 in 2017, and those roots stay valid until 2036 and 2039. 26 of the 29 bundle packages contain at least one root that Mozilla has removed from its programme and that is still inside its validity period. Matching exact fingerprints against CCADB’s records gives 95 such roots across those packages.

eMudhra issued the compromised intermediates from its emSign Root TLS CA - G3, which emSign ECC Root CA - G3 cross-signs. Root TLS CA - G3 itself is in none of the scanned bundles, so the cross-signing root is the one that matters here. Sectigo also cross-signed each intermediate from its AAA Certificate Services root, a 2004 Comodo certificate valid until 2028. A client that uses a bundle containing emSign ECC Root CA - G3 or AAA Certificate Services as its trust anchors, and skips revocation checks, will accept a chain running from a leaf through a compromised intermediate to that root, because the attacker supplies the intermediates in the TLS handshake.

Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 in response to the incident, as its 20 October notice records, so it is one of the 95. The root is in ten of the packages I scanned: Excon, Stripe’s Ruby and PHP libraries, gRPC for Ruby, PHP and Python, Composer’s ca-bundle, gocertifi, App Engine’s API stubs and virtualenv. certifi carried it through 2026.7.22 and dropped it in 2026.10.18, a day before the 2026.10.19 release in the fix table, and a lockfile pinned to 2026.7.22 or another release that included it still installs it.

Mozilla ended AAA’s TLS trust in 2025, and certifi dropped it in 2025.4.26. It isn’t among the 95 above, which only counts certificates Mozilla removed from its programme outright. It’s still in 17 of the packages I scanned, including honeybadger, httpclient, aws-sdk-v1, Guzzle 3, algoliasearch, nap, gocertifi, httplib2 and botocore’s fallback. Honeybadger, httpclient on MRI, aws-sdk-v1 and Guzzle 3 use that file as the trust anchor by default, and algoliasearch adds it to an existing store, while the other twelve use it as a fallback or when code selects it.

pip 26.2.2 vendors certifi 2026.10.19, which contains neither root. botocore merged a fix removing AAA from its fallback bundle on 20 October, but the latest botocore release still ships it. AWS updated aws-sdk-core’s 2018 bundle the same day the issue was reported and Excon replaced its bundle in 1.8.0, released on 21 October, while gRPC’s backport is still open.
Package metadata

Finding all of this took downloading and parsing every file in nearly seven thousand archives, because the only record of a bundled trust store is the file itself. The manifest, lockfile and SBOM for an app using httpclient record httpclient 2.9.0, a checksum, and pkg:gem/[email protected]. What the app depends on for TLS is Mozilla’s root list as it stood in 2014, and those documents record it only as httpclient’s name and version. When a root gets pulled, vulnerability scanners and dependency bots downstream match on those names and versions, so a search for “contains AAA Certificate Services” has to start from archive contents.

Vlad Miricioiu describes the same gap for compiled code in Binary Dependencies: Identifying the Hidden Packages We All Depend On. A Python wheel that bundles a precompiled C library depends on that library, “even though these dependency relationships are invisible to us”, because the wheel’s metadata lists only its Python dependencies. A CA bundle is what he calls a phantom binary dependency, with a PEM file in place of a .so. It’s third-party data, maintained upstream by Mozilla’s root programme on its own release schedule, copied into a package by hand at some point and then carried forward through every release after.

When an application depends on certifi directly, its lockfile names certifi and a version, and tools can track it. pip vendors certifi and records the version in src/pip/_vendor/vendor.txt, but that file is a convention of pip’s source repository, and the installed wheel’s metadata lists pip alone. webpki-roots shows up in uv’s Cargo.lock, but the uv binary you install from PyPI or Homebrew ships as a single executable with the roots compiled in and the lockfile left behind.

A file called cacert.pem inside a gem appears only in the archive’s file listing, and finding out which roots it holds means parsing it. Few registry schemas have a field for “this package vendors a copy of X at version Y”. Debian’s Built-Using field records statically linked sources, and CycloneDX’s pedigree records where a component’s contents came from. The generators that produce most SBOMs build from lockfiles, so httpclient’s entry records httpclient 2.9.0 and omits the 2014 root list inside it.

blocks.text: I’ve mentioned before my interest in the history and development of nuclear weapons.
Currently, I’m reading The Doomsday Machine: Confessions of a Nuclear War Planner by Daniel Ellsberg (of Pentagon Papers renown).
In the first chapter, Ellsberg talks about his time working at the RAND Corporation during the missile gap years when the U.S. thought it was falling behind the Soviet Union in nuclear capabilities.
Many of his descriptions sound strikingly similar to the rhetoric coming out of places like Anthropic. For example, note the religious overtones of working at a corporation:

I loved RAND, where I ended up spending ten years [...] Much, I imagined, like members of a religious order would, I shared with my colleagues a sense of brotherhood, living and working with others for a transcendent cause.
They were insiders: burdened with the responsibility of knowledge others did not possess.

precisely in my early missile-gap years at RAND and as a consultant in Washington, there was our sense of mission, the burden of believing we knew more about the dangers ahead, and what might be done about them, than did the generals in the Pentagon or SAC, or Congress or the public, or even the president. It was an enlivening burden.
And what was their “enlivening burden”? Saving the world:
[My colleagues] shared a feeling—soon transmitted to me—that we were in the most literal sense working to save the world.
What really stood out was this part, where Ellsberg describes how he and his colleagues truly believed the end was nigh:

From the Air Force intelligence estimates I was newly privy to, and the dark view of the Soviets, which my colleagues shared with the whole national security community, I couldn't believe that the world would long escape nuclear holocaust. Alain Enthoven and I were the youngest members of the department. Neither of us joined the extremely generous retirement plan RAND offered. Neither of us believed, in our late twenties, we had a chance of collecting on it.
This reminds me of the report that AI researchers have taken up smoking as a way to signal their belief that AI will cure cancer before smoking kills them.

At this point, I wouldn’t be surprised to hear a lab like Anthropic announce they’re discontinuing all employer-sponsored retirement benefits. It’d be a small sacrifice on behalf of the employees to demonstrate their faith that universal high income is just around the corner. (The corporate cost savings would just be a nice bonus.)

Alain Enthoven and I were the youngest members of the department. Neither of us joined the extremely generous retirement plan RAND offered. Neither of us believed, in our late twenties, we had a chance of collecting on it.
This reminds me of the report that AI researchers have taken up smoking as a way to signal their belief that AI will cure cancer before smoking kills them.

At this point, I wouldn’t be surprised to hear a lab like Anthropic announce they’re discontinuing all employer-sponsored retirement benefits. It’d be a small sacrifice on behalf of the employees to demonstrate their faith that universal high income is just around the corner. (The corporate cost savings would just be a nice bonus.)

blocks.text: It was 52 years ago this month, in October 1974, that Creative Computing, one of the greatest computer magazines of the 1970s and 1980s, made its debut.
Origins at Digital Equipment Corporation

Competing with Byte magazine was tough, even though Creative Computing actually beat Byte to market by several months. The only way a general purpose computing magazine could really do it was by taking a different angle. That was the secret of Creative Computing‘s success.

The idea came to its founder, David Ahl, when he was working at Digital Equipment Corporation. Ahl started at DEC in 1970, and part of his job was publishing a computer newsletter aimed at educators. Its circulation was 7-10 times larger than the number of computers DEC had sold into the educational market. He learned that people who used other computers were subscribing to his newsletter and adapting it to whatever platforms they used.

Ahl recognized an opportunity, and he also recognized DEC was going to completely miss it. In spite of him having evidence to the contrary, DEC CEO Ken Olsen insisted there was no market for a computer for individuals. As a result, Ahl left DEC, briefly taking a job at AT&T until the time was right for him to launch a magazine.

He started receiving subscription requests even before the magazine was ready to launch. This gave him enough capital to print additional issues and send them to schools and libraries where other potential subscribers would be likely to see copies. This worked, allowing him to quickly build circulation. Then, in 1977, the first microcomputers hit the market in the form of the Apple II, Commodore PET, and Radio Shack TRS-80, providing another growth opportunity.
By 1978, it had 60,000 subscribers and nearly $1 million in revenue.
What made Creative Computing different?

David Ahl’s background was in education, and his experience showed in his newsletter he published at DEC, and that continued at Creative Computing. Byte‘s target audience was hobbyists and engineers, where Creative Computing targeted people looking to use a computer as an educational aid. There was certainly overlap in the two magazines’ readership, but the differences made it easier for the two magazines to coexist. Some people would be much more comfortable reading one over the other, and some authors would be much more comfortable writing for one than the other.

Creative Computing covered everything, and reading its issues from the late 1970s is enlightening. Today, we think of a world where kit computers gave way to pre-built computers, and the Apple II, Commodore PET, and Radio Shack TRS-80 took over the world. Flipping through the pages of Creative Computing shows that wasn’t the case at all. The kit computers and the pre-built computers coexisted for a number of years. Not only that, various other companies did attempt to compete. Flipping through the pages of Creative Computing, you can see the product announcements for those systems, some occasional editorial coverage, and advertising. Two obscure systems they covered include the Imagination Machine and the Interact.

Most of these systems didn’t become popular enough to end up with their own magazines covering them. But Creative Computing gave them coverage for as long as they remained viable. If you are a fan of overlooked platforms from late 1970s and early 1980s, Creative Computing is a must read. Not only is it likely they covered things Byte missed, its perspective of the things Byte did cover was different.
Type in programs

One of the hallmarks of Creative Computing was its type-in programs. Like the rest of the magazine, the type-ins were generally not machine specific, but instead were frequently written in a way that they could run on a variety of platforms with little or no modification. It meant the programs could be a bit bland, but it also left plenty of room for you to customize the software yourself to take advantage of the machine you had.

One example was its 1978 publication of the game Oregon Trail, in the May-June issue. It wasn’t the same as the commercial version of the game marketed for the Apple II. This was a completely text-based version, based on earlier code that had run on minicomputers since 1971. It was simple enough you could adapt it for pretty much any home computer’s version of Basic, as long as it had enough memory. The catch was, the program was around 18K in size. But as long as you had 24K or more of RAM, customizing the game would have been a fun project.
For that matter, abbreviated versions for computers with less RAM soon appeared, presumably based on that code. I played a version called Westward Ho, developed for the Commodore PET.
That 1978 version of Oregon Trail is available on Github if you want to study it or use it.

Another Creative Computing type-in that became widely circulated and adapted was Super Star Trek, published in the May-June 1975 issue. This was a turn-based strategy game where you played the captain of the starship Enterprise, patrolling the federation space and fighting off Klingon invaders. I played a later conversion of the game for the Commodore 64 by Don Lekei that added color, sound, animation, and graphics.
Selling out to Ziff-Davis

As the computer market grew, it became increasingly difficult for an independent publication to compete with the larger publishers. In addition, most of those larger publishers were interested in acquiring at least one of those independent publications, as that would be much more cost effective than trying to launch a new magazine into this market. As a result, Creative Computing sold out to Ziff Davis in 1982, the company that would later publish magazines like PC Magazine and Computer Shopper.
Ziff Davis shut down Creative Computing‘s side businesses selling software and peripherals, preferring to concentrate solely on being a magazine and to not compete with any of its advertisers.

Creative Computing had a good run, lasting a little over 10 years, folding after the December 1985 issue. By 1985, the general purpose computing magazines were struggling. The industry had moved on to platform-specific magazines. Someone who was on the fence about what computer to buy might subscribe to a general purpose magazine, but after they made the decision, they were likely to drop the magazine in favor of a magazine like 80 Micro or RUN that was fully dedicated to whatever machine they had, or at least splitting coverage with another computer of the same brand.
Creative Computing as a historical reference

If pre-1985 computer history interests you, Creative Computing is essential reading. Not only did it cover platforms that didn’t necessarily get a lot of coverage elsewhere, it could also be pretty outspoken about the systems that ultimately won. For example, David Ahl called the IBM PC and PCjr mediocre. He said they would probably win, but we didn’t have to be happy about that. Although the PCjr was not successful, its close relative, the Tandy 1000, definitely was.
In addition, David Ahl’s analysis of companies who failed is valuable. His perspective was a bit different from many other computer journalists, having worked at a computer company himself.
The complete run of Creative Computing is available at the Internet Archive.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
